The Architecture of Capabilities: Concerns That Cooperate, Ambitions to Be Wrong

The owner, 2026-10-29: "can you build an architecture document that organizes all of our capabilities into a structure that cooperates on concerns and ambitions to be wrong?" And then, alone: "][tests][".

This is that map. Every capability Everland Ghostsong has is placed in one of seven rings, by the concern it serves. Each says what it believes, how it could be wrong, where we would see that, and what turns it off. Between every two rings stand the tests. The system-level wiring (servers, databases, modules) is in architecture.md; this document is about how the parts think together. The board of what is built is docs/next-compile-status.md (scripts/issue-status-board).

The core rule: ][tests][

The brackets face outward. The tests are not inside any one part: they stand between the parts, at every seam, holding two capabilities together. A capability may be as clever as it likes inside; where it hands something to another, a test says what is handed and checks it. So a part being wrong is found at the edge where it would hurt a neighbour, by a check that belongs to neither. Two cases from 2026-10-28 and 10-29:

  • The Lua load test, which checks the seam between the project's scripts and the game's script engine, found that the buddy levers' list shared a file name with its code, and the engine would refuse one.
  • The comparison of the six ways to find a path, which checks the seam between pathfinding and the bots' own steering, found that A* and "learn the map" wobbled at over 100 degrees a yard. Neither part's own test could have seen either fault.

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. The risk is a seam left bare. Every part passes its own tests, and the fault lives where two of them meet, unseen until a player finds it.

  • When two capabilities first touch, write the seam's test then, while both are fresh.
  • When a fault is found at a seam, keep the test that would have caught it.
  • Count the cards below that say "no seam test yet", and let the number fall.

The shape: seven rings

From what is, to what we see. Each ring uses the one before it and never overrides it.

Ring Its concern It answers
1. Ground the world as the game's own files say it is what is there?
2. Knowledge what our tools work out and our bots learn about the ground what do we believe about it?
3. Rules the game as we changed it what is allowed, and what happens?
4. Minds what bots and characters decide what does each one choose to do?
5. Bodies how a decision becomes action in the running server how is it done?
6. Views what a person sees of all this, without logging in what is happening, and how does it look?
7. Operations how it is built, run, kept and shared how does it reach the world, and stay well?

The tests sit in the seams between every pair, and wrap the whole (the quick tests at each compile, the tests of each commit). How it may turn out, and how to steer it. The rings stay useful while each capability sits plainly in one. The drift to watch is a part reaching across two rings: a mind that rewrites knowledge, or a view that decides. When a card is hard to place, split the capability at its seam, and put a test there.

The contracts: how the rings cooperate

Rules every capability keeps with its neighbours. Each was learned, most of them by being wrong first.

  1. The ground decides. No belief overrides what is there: every planner's pick is checked against the navigation mesh before a bot walks it (617o1, "the mesh decides"), and the painted map learns only from the world's own refusals. Knowledge is a guess about the ground, never a replacement for it.
  2. One core, three bodies. A behaviour's thinking is written once as plain arithmetic with no server code (the roaming core, the following core, the five ways, the painted map). It is then:
    • tested alone, offline;
    • worn by the server, through thin glue;
    • mirrored in a sandbox page, step for step, run on the same courses with the same random numbers so the numbers read side by side.

    What the owner watches on a page is what the buddies do.

  3. Data made apart from data viewed. Generators write data; viewers only read it (the zone data and the zone renderer, the ground and the sandbox, the roads and the battleground page). A viewer's bug can't corrupt data, and a generator's fault shows in the data, where a test can read it.
  4. Patches round-trip. Our changes to the server, its modules and its Lua engine are scripts that apply and undo. The source tree goes back to upstream after every build, so upstream can move and our changes re-derive (the patch system; test-source-patches, test-patch-undo-order).
  5. Headers are the registry. A patch's or test's own header says which profiles take it, in what order, and whether it is a quick test. No shared list to fall out of step (189; test-patch-headers, test-patch-lists-current).
  6. Built is not on. Every new behaviour comes behind a switch that starts off: a module setting, a profile's patch, a command. Being built and being on are separate decisions, and the board shows both (the design target in CLAUDE.md).
  7. Refusal teaches. The world's "no" is data:
    • a refused step paints a wall on the painted map, for every bot;
    • "learn the map" learns the cell;
    • the stuck rule backs out twice as far each time.

    Nothing pushes against the same thing for ever.

  8. One map, many hands. Knowledge is shared at the widest scope it holds true for: the painted map is one per region and every buddy there paints it; the explorers' paint is per clan per area. A lesson one bot learns, all of them know.
  9. Every picture kept, every run receipted. Each screenshot is filed with what made it, what changed, and what it shows (development-history/). Programs that run unattended write a goodbye receipt of what they did. The record of being wrong is kept as carefully as the record of being right.

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. Contracts erode quietly, one convenience at a time:

  • a generator someone hand-edits once;
  • a switch turned on by default "just for testing";
  • a page that computes something the core does not.

When a contract is broken on purpose, change it here first, with why. When it is broken by accident, the seam test that missed it is the next thing to write.

The method: ambitions to be wrong

The aim is not to be right first. It is to be wrong early, cheaply, and visibly, and to keep what was learned.

  • Race alternatives. When the right design is unknown, build several and run them on the same ground: five ways to find a path, then six (617o7, 617o8); the battleground's open questions each built two ways behind a switch (176a2). The race decides, not the argument.
  • Measure before believing. A capability gets a number that would embarrass it: degrees turned a yard, bumps by round of trips, yards kept from walls, plans a millisecond. The turning measure, added for the painted map, caught A*'s wobble the same hour.
  • Undo on numbers, and keep the note. An idea that measures worse is taken out and its numbers written where it was. Choosing the least-walked waypoints made spacing worse, so it was undone; the template and 617o8 say why, so nobody tries it blind again.
  • Make the call, then ask. A design question that would stop work is answered with the agent's best call, written down with why, for the owner to curate (CLAUDE.md, the design target). A wrong call costs a revert; a stopped day costs a day.
  • Prefer an error to a fallback. A fallback hides being wrong. Where something can't be done, it says so, with what was done before it stopped (the owner's standing rule).

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. Racing and measuring can turn into collecting numbers for their own sake. The owner said so on 2026-10-29: "the goal of our interactions is the creation of a product, not the generation of additional unique datas." So:

  • each race ends in a decision that is written down, the losers kept behind their switch or undone;
  • a measurement earns its place only when it can change what is built next.

Common patterns, and guiding each to a good turnout

The same eight shapes recur across the rings. Each has a typical way of going wrong, a sign that shows it early, and a way to steer.

  1. Twins. One behaviour written as a core, worn by the server and mirrored on a page.
    • Goes wrong by drifting, so the page shows what the game no longer does.
    • The sign is a page number that moves when the core's test didn't.
    • Steer by running the same courses with the same random numbers on both, and by changing the core first.
  2. Learning from refusal. The painted map, "learn the map", the stuck rule.
    • Goes wrong by over-learning: a bot painting itself in, a wall that is really open, a fact that stays after the world changed.
    • The sign is plans that find no way, or a region whose walls only grow.
    • Steer by never painting a bot's own place, squeezing out when boxed in, and next, unlearning: a wall nobody has bumped for a long time fades back to unknown.
  3. Generated, not written. Zone data, help rows, references, lists, boards, pages.
    • Goes wrong by going stale, since the generated file is right only when made.
    • The sign is a test that regenerates and compares, failing.
    • Steer by giving every generated file a line naming its maker, and a quick test that remakes it.
  4. Races. Several designs on the same ground.
    • Goes wrong by mistaking noise for a difference (the trails runs varied more from run to run than between settings).
    • The sign is a winner that changes on a second run.
    • Steer by running each setting at least twice, and calling a winner only when the gap is wider than the spread.
  5. Switches. Built is not on.
    • Goes wrong by sprawl: switches nobody remembers, paths nobody runs.
    • The sign is a switch left off for many compiles.
    • Steer by listing every switch on the board, and asking about any left off for three compiles: turn it on, or take it out.
  6. Shared ground. Many agents, one folder.
    • Goes wrong by collision, or by a silent failure (a commit tool that printed nothing and committed nothing).
    • The sign is uncommitted work that nobody claims.
    • Steer by claiming before editing, committing small and often, checking each commit landed, and saying who holds what.
  7. The owner's words as the specification. Every behaviour starts from the owner's sentences, kept word for word.
    • Goes wrong by misreading, or by reading too literally.
    • The sign is a design the owner corrects ("notice how I said *less than*").
    • Steer by keeping the words beside the reading, acting on the best reading, and showing the result early, so a misreading costs an hour, not a week.
  8. Offline first, server later. A core checked alone, the server's glue written blind until the owner compiles.
    • Goes wrong by piling up uncompiled work.
    • The sign is a growing "waiting for the compile" row on the board.
    • Steer by syntax-checking the glue against the server's headers, keeping it thin, and trying each new switch first on a branch realm with the army.

The capabilities, ring by ring

Each card: what it claims; what would prove it wrong; where we would see that; and what turns it off. Numbers in brackets are issues.

1. Ground

Capability Claims Wrong if Seen in Off
Map files: heights, areas, water (data-files/maps) the shape of the land, and which area each square is heights or areas misread test-zone-maps, test-ground-decode (always on: it is the world)
Navigation mesh (data-files/mmaps) where a body can stand and walk a walkable route refused, or a wall walked through test-navmesh-caves, refusals counted in game (always on)
Collision models (data-files/vmaps) the trees, rocks and buildings that block a doodad missing, or a ghost one the sandbox's refused steps (always on)
The world database (acore_world_*) every creature, quest, item and spawn a row disagreeing with the client test-quest-reward-has-a-giver, test-sql-mirror per profile

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. The ground is the steadiest ring, and it fails all at once when it fails: a client update, a map file read with the wrong layout, a mesh built for another version.

  • Treat its files as read-only, and every reader as a tested decoder.
  • When a reading looks wrong, suspect the reader before the world.

2. Knowledge

Capability Claims Wrong if Seen in Off
Zone data (617e14b) every zone's squares and sub-zones, the open sea left out a zone cut wrong, sea counted as land test-zone-maps, test-render-zone regenerated, not switched
Area middles and sub-areas (617e2, 617e12) each area's centre, and its parts by monsters and steep edges a part that can't be walked to test-buddy-subareas per area
Grids, rooms and baked distance maps (617o2, 617o3) the walkable cells and their walking distances a cell the mesh refuses test-exploration-engine per mode
The painted map (617o8) what the bots have walked and bumped, shared, kept between runs bumps not falling over trips; a gap shut that is open test-paint-paths, test-buddy-paint-paths (bumps by round, round trip) .buddy path (mesh is the default)
Roads and crossings (176a2c) the battleground's roads as a graph, taken in turn a squad going back the way it came test-arathi-basin-rules the scene's settings
Levers and the semantic map (638) about 1,400 small things a buddy can do with its body, grouped by meaning a lever the game won't do; a group that mixes meanings test-buddy-levers, test-lua-unique-names .lever (game masters)

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. Knowledge grows. That is its point and its danger: a belief that was true when made outlives the ground it was made from.

  • Name each fact's maker and date.
  • Remake facts rather than patch them.
  • Give learned knowledge a way to forget (the painted map's walls should fade when unbumped; question 1 of 617o8 keeps them).
  • Prefer a little knowledge that is surely right to a lot that may be wrong.

3. Rules

Capability Claims Wrong if Seen in Off
Profiles and their caps (155, the profile pages) each profile's level range and rules a setting on the wrong profile test-profile-config-gates, test-profile-tables-agree the profile chosen
The empty world and ambushes (phase 2, 3) monsters come to the player, 120 to 160 yards out, on a random walk of seconds spawns too near, too regular test-ambush, test-datapath-ambush the Lua scripts' load
Treasure and the economy (phase 4) value flows back into chests items duplicated or lost test-treasure the scripts
Travelers (phase 5) strangers wander between places travellers stuck test-travel the scripts
Classes, talents and quests (phase 7) each class's custom spells, talents every third of a level a spell unlearnable, a point lost test-talent-builds, test-spell-designs, test-racial-quests per profile
Progression and endgame (phase 8) gear tiers, legendaries, world bosses a tier skipped test-basic-legendaries, test-world-boss-countdown, test-gearsets per profile

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. Rules multiply across profiles, and their danger is meeting each other: a level cap, a talent rule and a drop table each fine alone, wrong together.

  • Keep rules as data with a gate per profile.
  • Test the gates, not just each rule (test-profile-config-gates).
  • When two rules fight, write which wins into the profile's page.

Parties and the dungeon draw (617c2, 617c3) buddies group by distance; a dungeon draws a balanced party a buddy ungrouped beside a full party; no healer no seam test yet: seen only in game per place
Gear, gems, loot and spells (617a, 617j, 617n) buddies dress, gem and learn by their talent plan a socket left empty, a weapon unskilled test-buddy-kit, test-buddy-gems, test-buddy-talents per command

Battleground squads and fronts (176a2, 629) trios on the roads; fronts that hold lines squads clumping; lines breaking test-arathi-basin-rules, test-battleground-front the scene
Sargobras and the narrators (E066, phase 9) a guide who answers by whispers a choice made differently from his menus test-sargobras-follow, test-narrators the patch

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. Minds misbehave as crowds, not one by one: bunching, knots on a ledge, walking in rings, wobbling. Each bot does something sensible, and together it looks wrong.

  • Judge minds by crowd measures (spacing, coverage, stuck, turning) on the same ground as a baseline.
  • Fix the cause in the mind, never by hiding the symptom in steering.
  • Watch the picture as well as the number: the owner's eye caught the rubbing before any measure did.

5. Bodies

Capability Claims Wrong if Seen in Off
The buddy module, C++ (B036) the minds above, in the server a crash, a call on a character not yet in the world test-buddy-made-out-of-world, test-patched-syntax, the owner's compile the module's settings
The bot module and its patches (mod-playerbots, B0xx) bots that fight, loot and take orders a buddy taking another's orders test-compile-module-set, test-source-patches per patch
Lua scripts on the game's engine (ALE, src/lua-*) fast-changing rules without a compile two files one name; a missing global test-beta-lua-load, test-lua-globals, test-lua-unique-names, test-ale-method-names the profile's Lua folder
Settings and install steps (C0xx, E0xx) each profile's values and its setup a value on the wrong profile; a step out of order test-profile-config-gates, test-patch-plan, test-patch-undo-order the patch's header

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. Bodies fail loudly (a crash, a refused login) or quietly (an order the server ignores). The glue is where they hide.

  • Keep the glue thin, and the thinking in the cores.
  • Syntax-check every change against the server's headers before the compile.
  • Start each new switch off, try it on a branch realm first, and read the server's log after.

Capability Claims Wrong if Seen in Off
The ground sandbox (617e16) bots on real ground, any way, any area, measured the page and the game disagree the page's measures, pictures, test-ground-decode (a page)
The battleground sandbox (617e16l) two sides playing Arathi Basin as the bots would squads not on the roads its pictures (a page)
Zone renders, gearset gallery, lever map the world, the gear and the levers seen whole a render that differs from the data test-render-zone, test-gear-designs (pages)

The GM command reference every command, its level and words a command undescribed test-gm-command-reference (generated)
The board (CLAUDE.md, the design target) where every issue stands an issue on the wrong row read at each compile (generated)
Development history every picture, with its story a picture without notes test-file-screenshot (always kept)
Pictures drawn as light (the gif tools) an idea drawn as a short animated gif, by the sibling gif generator's own code a gif that shows something other than its idea the contact sheet, by eye; development-history/ (tools: compose-architecture-gifs, render-gif-scores)

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. Views are how the owner decides, so a view that flatters is worse than none.

  • Show the measures that can embarrass a capability, beside the picture.
  • Keep every picture, wrong ones included.
  • Make each view from data a generator wrote, so the view can't invent.
  • When a view and the game disagree, believe the game, and mend the twin.

Patch runner and plan (189) each profile's patches, in order, from their headers a patch on the wrong profile test-patch-plan, test-carried-files headers

Dormant work (dormant/) built work parked whole, with its history and a note on how to wake it, out of every build, test and hook something there still run, or woken without its note each folder's README (nothing runs it)

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. Operations decay at their edges: a hook missing after a fresh clone, a test that fails after every commit and is stopped being read, a tool that fails in silence.

  • Read the commit tests' reports, and fix a failure the day it appears (three had been failing since the day before; two were this session's own).
  • Make every tool say what it did.
  • Keep the board current at each compile.
  • Park what nobody will reach for in dormant/, whole, rather than leave it half-used among the working tools; wake it when a use returns.

Where the rings are thinnest

These are the gaps, not the strengths: where being wrong is most likely and least seen.

  • Minds without a compile. The path switch, the painted map in game, the army and stand-in grouping are written and checked offline, but no buddy has walked them yet. The first compile is their first real test.
  • Knowledge kept but never forgotten. The painted map learns walls and keeps them. A doodad that moves, or a wall painted wrongly, stays until the region's file is removed. Nothing yet unlearns.
  • Pages that run their own copy. The sandboxes run the script twin, not the server. The twin is held to the C++ by shared courses (test-buddy-paint-paths), but only for the parts both have.
  • Seams with no test. The dungeon draw and party grouping are seen only in game; the transcripts' bundling only by its hook. A card that says "no seam test yet" is a place to put one.
  • Minds that choose by fixed lists. A buddy answers each concern (an ally hurt, enemies close) with the first ability of a fixed list for one guessed talent tree. Its talents, its other trees, its mana, the fight's movement and its cooldowns change nothing yet (planned: 625a to 625e).
  • Issues with no Current Behavior. 42 open issues say nothing of where they stand, so the board can't place them.

How it may turn out, and how to steer it. These are the next things to build, in this order, because each makes the others safer:

  1. Compile, and walk the path switch, the painted map and the army on the test realm.
  2. Let painted walls fade when nobody has bumped them for a long time.
  3. A seam test for the dungeon draw and party grouping, on stand-ins.
  4. A sentence of Current Behavior in each of the 42 silent issues, so the board can place them.

Keeping this document true

It names tests, not numbers, so it stays true while numbers move: run the named test for the current figure. When a capability is added:

  1. Give it a card in its ring.
  2. Name the test at its seam, or write one.
  3. Say what turns it off.

When a contract above is broken and kept broken on purpose, the contract changes here first.
